Exergame programmes and exercise motivation in randomized trials published since 2024: a systematic review

Corrections left visible in place, each marked “Corrected after audit”: the abstract and §4.1 now state the null between-group result of the trial recoded to other and say the count of trials favouring the exergame arm depends on two recodes the user has not individually ruled on (H1); §3.8 no longer says every difference was on autonomous forms of motivation (H2); the abstract’s with-and-without sentence (M1); the “only trial” sentence in §3.4 (M2); a column without the high-risk trials added to the §4.1 table (M3); the as-treated analysis of one trial stated in §3.3 and §3.4 (M4); a research implication moved to the review’s own limitations (M5); eight smaller wordings (L2 to L8).

This review was conducted by an automated agent pipeline. Searching, screening, data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment were done by language-model agents. A person (the user who commissioned it) approved the protocol and the inclusion set and ruled on the questions the agents escalated. No second human screened any record. conduct-disclosure.md says what was automated and what a person must still do.

Abstract

Background. “Exercise video games and motivation” is a topic and not a question. The question this review answers, approved by the user before any searching, is narrower: in randomized trials first reported from 2024 onward, does an exergame programme of two weeks or more change motivation for exercise, on a named multi-item instrument, against an arm with no exergame, and how far can that evidence be trusted?

Methods. PubMed and OpenAlex were searched on 2026-11-28, with one pass of backward citation searching. Two agents screened every record independently at title and abstract and at full text. Full texts were retrieved by open-access routes only. Each included trial was extracted by one agent and its risk of bias rated with RoB 2 by two agents independently, with an adjudicator for disagreements. The synthesis is narrative, following SWiM; no meta-analysis was run.

Results. 189 database records and 10 from citation searching were identified; 140 and 10 were screened; 65 reports were sought and 21 could not be retrieved; 44 were assessed in full text; 6 trials (6 reports) were included. One of the six is kept marked as of doubtful eligibility by the user’s decision. Four trials were rated at high risk of bias overall and two at some concerns; none was rated low in any domain. By each trial’s own between-group test at the end of the programme, two trials favoured the exergame arm (one against no intervention, one against conventional training on one of four subscales), one was mixed across subscales, and three reported only a total score whose construction or direction the paper does not state, so no direction was coded for them. Both trials coded as favouring the exergame arm are rated at high risk of bias. Setting the doubtful trial aside changes none of these counts except that two, not three, trials have no coded direction. [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] Of the three with no coded direction, one, a trial not rated high, reported no difference between arms on its total score (between-group P read as 0.936); one reported a difference in change scores but not in final scores; one is the doubtful trial. The count of two favouring depends on two direction codes that were changed during appraisal under a rule the user adopted for another trial, and on which the user has not ruled individually; as first coded, three trials favoured the exergame arm, one showed no between-group difference, one was mixed and one had no coded direction. Setting the doubtful trial aside leaves the direction counts unchanged except that two, not three, trials have no coded direction, and three of five, not four of six, are at high risk of bias.

Conclusion. The included trials do not show whether exergame programmes change exercise motivation. Certainty is very low. The answer rests on six small open-access trials; 21 reports that might have been eligible could not be read.

Registration. Not registered. Funding and interests. To be declared by the person responsible for the review.

1. Background and objectives

Exergames, video games played by moving the body, are often proposed as a way to make exercise something people want to do [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] (“often” removed: no source was consulted for how often). Whether they do is an empirical question about motivation, and motivation is measured in many ways: as enjoyment, as attendance, as a single rating, or with multi-item instruments built on a theory of motivation. This review makes no claim about what is already known; no source was consulted for one.

Objective. In randomized controlled trials whose first results report was published on or after 2024-01-01, does an exergame programme lasting two weeks or more change participants’ motivation for exercise, measured with a named multi-item motivation instrument, compared with an arm that has no exergame, and how much can that evidence be trusted?

The user asked “What is the current state of exercise video games and motivation?” and approved the question above as its operational form at the first gate. What that narrowing leaves out is stated in section 4.3. It is not a map of the field.

2. Methods

The protocol (protocol.md) was written and approved before any search ran. This section summarizes it. Reporting follows PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021) and, for the synthesis, SWiM (Campbell et al., 2020).

2.1 Eligibility

Framework: PICOS. A report was included if it met all of these, and excluded under the mirror code (E1 to E8) of the lowest-numbered criterion it failed, or E9 if it was not a primary report.

Code Criterion
I1 At least one arm receives an exergame: a digital game in which the player’s movement of limbs or trunk is the game input and the game has a goal or score
I2 Participants or clusters were allocated to arms at random
I3 At least one arm receives no exergame
I4 The exergame arm was scheduled to last two weeks or more
I5 Motivation for exercise, physical activity or the training activity was measured with a named multi-item self-report instrument or subscale
I6 Results on that instrument are given for the exergame arm and a non-exergame arm after baseline
I7 The trial’s first results report was published on or after 2024-01-01
I8 The full text is in English

Enjoyment measured alone, single-item ratings, adherence and interviews do not meet I5. Trials comparing one exergame with another are excluded (E3). Need-satisfaction scales and the interest/enjoyment subscale of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory count as motivation measures. The full cases on each side of every line are in protocol.md section 2. Studies were grouped for synthesis by comparator, population, platform and instrument.

2.2 Sources and search

Source Interface Last searched Matched Retrieved
PubMed NCBI E-utilities 2026-11-28 83 83
OpenAlex REST API, keyless 2026-11-28 106 106
Reference lists of included reports OpenAlex referenced_works 2026-11-28 255 references listed, 10 new records taken 10

Each string combines an exergame block, a motivation block and a randomized-design block, limited to 2024-01-01 through 2026-11-28. The literal strings are in protocol.md section 4 and, as run, in search-log.md. OpenAlex applied stemming of its own, so its matching may be somewhat broader than the written string. Backward citation searching ran for one iteration from the six included reports, keeping references dated 2024 or later whose title carried an exergame term, at most 15 per seed. Forward citation searching was not run. PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL, trial registries and grey literature were not searched.

2.3 Selection

Two screener agents, given identical inputs and no access to each other’s decisions, screened every record at title and abstract and every retrieved report at full text. At title and abstract a record advanced if either screener answered include or unsure. Full-text disagreements went to an adjudicator agent, which decided from the saved text or escalated to the user. Every quotation a screener gave was checked by script against the saved text before its decisions were compared with the other’s.

Full texts were fetched by script from three open-access routes only: Europe PMC, arXiv, and (added after the second gate, amendment A2) open-access PDF copies listed by OpenAlex. A report that could not be fetched is counted as not retrieved, never as excluded on a criterion.

2.4 Data collection and data items

One extractor agent per study read the saved full text and recorded coded values from the protocol’s lists, and quoted, located numbers. It made no judgments. Two judge agents per study, independent of each other, could query any extracted value; an adjudicator settled queries from the paper’s text. The primary outcome was motivation at the end of the intervention, exergame arm against non-exergame arm, on the instrument meeting I5; secondary outcomes were the same at any later follow-up, and adherence. Other items are defined in protocol.md section 7.

direction records each trial’s own between-group test at the end of the intervention, coded from the reported test and not from the authors’ conclusion. It is not an effect size. A code of other here means the trial reported only a total or composite score and the paper does not state how it is formed in a way that fixes its direction (amendment A11), so no direction is coded and the quoted result is reported instead.

2.5 Risk of bias

RoB 2 (Sterne et al., 2019), applied to the motivation outcome at the end of the intervention, for the effect of assignment. The protocol fixes anchors for each domain (protocol.md section 8). Two judge agents rated every domain independently; an adjudicator decided ratings they gave differently, or escalated to the user where the anchor supported both. The overall rating is the worst domain, derived by script. Because motivation is self-reported by participants who know their arm, the protocol expected domain 4 to be some concerns at best for nearly every trial.

2.6 Synthesis, reporting bias and certainty

Narrative synthesis by thread; no meta-analysis, because the trials use different instruments and subscales in different populations and extraction was by machine. There is therefore no effect measure, no pooled estimate, no heterogeneity statistic and no forest plot. Directions are tabulated as counts with the risk-of-bias rating beside them. Counting directions is a weak method: it weights a trial of 25 the same as a trial of 66, and it is labelled as such where used.

Conclusions are stated with and without trials rated high overall, and with and without the trial of doubtful eligibility. Reporting bias was assessed only through domain 5 of RoB 2; no registry was searched. Certainty was rated per outcome with GRADE. Every included study is tier A (full text read); no claim below rests on an abstract.

2.7 Amendments to the protocol

All thirteen are dated 2026-11-28, and are in protocol.md section 14 with reasons.

# Change Approved
A1 E5 may be cited at title and abstract only when the abstract itself shows there is no eligible instrument Made by the pipeline during calibration; ratified by the user at gate 2
A2 A third full-text route: open-access PDF copies listed by OpenAlex User, gate 2
A3 Random allocation followed by reassignment of a minority at their own request, and allocation described as random but constrained or pseudo-randomized, count as randomized; the weakness is carried by risk of bias User, gate 2
A4 A movement-training system that scores the player against target movements is an exergame User, gate 2

Two consequences of the gate 3 amendments went beyond the items the user ruled on, and are stated here and in the conduct disclosure. Under A10, the domain 5 rating both judges had given oa-W7220097264 (high) was sent back and re-rated, as the user instructed. Under A11, the direction codes of two other trials that report only a total score (pm-40567995, pm-43021294) were sent back by the pipeline to two fresh judge agents per study, without a specific instruction from the user, so that the three such trials would be treated alike; all four queried the code and the adjudicator changed both to other. Before that, both original judges had accepted no between-group difference for pm-40567995 and favours exergame for pm-43021294. The user has not ruled on these two changes; every count below that depends on them says so.

3. Results

3.1 Study selection

The database searches identified 189 records (PubMed 83, OpenAlex 106). After 49 duplicates were removed, 140 were screened at title and abstract and 80 excluded, all by automation tools and none by a human reviewer. 60 reports were sought; 20 could not be retrieved; 40 were assessed in full text and 34 excluded: 22 for no named motivation instrument (E5), 8 for no exergame (E1), 2 for a programme under two weeks (E4), 1 for no motivation results by arm (E6) and 1 that was not a primary report (E9).

Citation searching identified 10 further records. None was removed before screening; 5 were excluded at title and abstract; 5 were sought, 1 was not retrieved, 4 were assessed and all 4 excluded (E4: 2; E5: 2).

Six studies, from six reports, were included, all from the database search.

These are two instances of one model; the number overstates what it would mean between two people. Reports not retrieved (21). None was excluded on a criterion and none was read. They are listed by name in gate-2.md section 7. Both screeners answered “include” for one of them at title and abstract (pm-42223906); for the rest at least one answered “unsure”.

3.3 Risk of bias

Figure 3. RoB 2 judgments per study and domain. Generated from rob.csv, 2026-11-28. Rows are labelled by study ID: oa-W7220097264 is Nikolova et al. (2025), pm-40567995 Huang et al. (2025), pm-41307454 Liu et al. (2025), pm-41628428 Ngo et al. (2026), pm-42974341 Anderson et al. (2026), pm-43021294 Tunc et al. (2026). The Overall column is derived as the worst domain. Of the three cells marked adjudicated, two (domain 5 of pm-40567995 and pm-43021294) were decided by the user under amendment A10; the data file has no separate label for a user ruling.

Figure 4. Number of studies at each judgment, per domain. Generated from rob.csv, 2026-11-28.

Four of the six trials are rated high overall and two some concerns (Huang et al., 2025; Ngo et al., 2026). No trial was rated low in any domain.

  • Missing outcome data (domain 3) is the most common reason for a high rating: three trials. In each, the exergame arm lost more participants than the comparator and the analysis was of completers (Anderson et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Tunc et al., 2026).
  • Randomization (domain 1) is high for one trial, whose paper states that allocation was not concealed and that one investigator enrolled and assigned participants (Anderson et al., 2026).
  • Deviations (domain 2) is high for one trial, which reports only a per-protocol analysis that dropped participants for low adherence (Tunc et al., 2026). [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] A second trial is rated some concerns in this domain and one judge called the rating close to high: its results are analysed by the arm participants actually joined, after seven changed arm at their own request. The paper says an analysis by original allocation gave consistent results and puts it in an appendix this review did not read (Ngo et al., 2026).
  • Measurement (domain 4) is some concerns for five trials, as the protocol expected for a self-reported outcome in unblinded participants. It is high for one, whose single motivation score is of unstated construction and has a mean above the maximum of the items as described (Nikolova et al., 2025).
  • Selection of the reported result (domain 5) is some concerns for all six. None shows a registration dated before enrolment that names the instrument and time point. Three report only a total score for an instrument whose subscales their Methods name; under amendment A10 that is some concerns and not high.

The judges agreed on 27 of 30 domain ratings (raw agreement 0.9, κ 0.737). The two judges are instances of one model, so this agreement overstates what it would mean between two people, and one of the 27 agreed pairs is the re-rated pair described at the end of this paragraph. Three were settled otherwise: one by the adjudicator and confirmed by the user’s amendment A13 (pm-41628428, domain 1), and two by the user’s ruling under A10 (pm-40567995 and pm-43021294, domain 5). The domain 5 rating of oa-W7220097264 was re-rated by two fresh agents after A10 and both gave some concerns; its overall rating stays high because of domain 4. The ruling under A10 decides one overall rating: pm-40567995 would be high overall had its domain 5 been rated high.

3.4 Thread 1: exergame against conventional exercise, and against no exercise

Rests on: six studies at tier A (full text). One of the six is of doubtful eligibility by the user’s decision. Directions are each trial’s own between-group test, not effect sizes, and the search probably missed trials that reported motivation only in the full text, which are more likely to be null.

Study Comparator Result at end of programme, as reported direction Overall risk of bias
Anderson et al. (2026) Wobble-board training IMI Interest/Enjoyment 5.04 ± 1.18 against 3.17 ± 1.31; the other three subscales not different (p 0.61, 0.81, 0.45) favours exergame High
Ngo et al. (2026) On-court tennis Game arm higher at post-test on intrinsic motivation to know (22.39 against 17.21) and to accomplish (21.82 against 18.41), and also on external regulation (23.11 against 18.24); four subscales not different mixed across subscales Some concerns
Huang et al. (2025) The same dance by video One BREQ-2 score per arm; between-group P read as 0.936 other Some concerns
Tunc et al. (2026) Conventional exercises MSPPA total: absolute scores at week 24 not different (p 0.13); change scores and ANCOVA different (p = 0.015 for the ANCOVA) other High
Nikolova et al. (2025) † “Traditional physical activity” One composite: 4.08 (0.52) against 3.15 (0.46), with a group effect and a time × group interaction other High
Liu et al. (2025) No intervention BREQ-2 intrinsic regulation 3.71 (0.94) to 4.81 (0.26) against 3.63 (0.86) to 3.76 (0.61); identified regulation also in favour; three subscales without a significant interaction favours exergame High

Against conventional exercise (five trials). One trial is coded as favouring the exergame arm, one as mixed and three have no coded direction. With the doubtful trial set aside the counts are one, one and two.

The one trial coded as favouring the game arm does so on one of four subscales of the IMI, measured once, after training, with no baseline, and it is rated high for both randomization and missing data (Anderson et al., 2026). The mixed trial found the game arm higher on two intrinsic-motivation subscales and also on external regulation, which the protocol counts as unfavourable; in that trial both arms’ intrinsic scores fell [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] both arms’ scores on intrinsic motivation to know and to accomplish fell over the 12 weeks, and the paper’s abstract describes the game arm as having retained intrinsic motivation better (Ngo et al., 2026). Its results are by the arm participants joined, not the arm they were allocated to (section 3.3). These two results do not contradict each other, and they do not confirm each other either: the instruments and the constructs differ.

For the three trials with no coded direction, the papers’ own conclusions are more favourable than their tables.

  • One concludes that its Kinect programme improved exercise behaviour regulation. The test that supports this is a within-group change in the game arm; the control arm moved the same way, and the between-group values in its Table 2 read as 0.936 and 1.000 (Huang et al., 2025). Which P values are the between-group ones is inferred from the table’s layout, because its footnote labels do not match the columns.
  • One describes motivation as maintained in the game arm and declining in the control arm. Its three between-group tests at the end of the programme do not agree, the control arm started higher (33.70 against 27.84), and the game arm’s change scores do not follow from its own means (Tunc et al., 2026).
  • One reports a clearly higher composite in the game arm. The composite’s mean exceeds the maximum of the items as the paper describes them, and how six subscales that run from amotivation to intrinsic regulation became one score is not stated (Nikolova et al., 2025). This is the doubtful trial. [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] Its game arm’s sessions also included group discussion, goal-setting and a personal activity plan; the paper describes nothing of the kind for the control arm, so the arms differ in more than the game.

Against no intervention (one trial; a single-study finding). A four-week programme on a game-driven exercise bike was followed by higher identified and intrinsic regulation than in a control arm that did nothing, by the time × group interaction (amendment A11 counts that test) (Liu et al., 2025). The trial is rated high for missing data: both dropouts came from the game arm. Its own limitations section says the interactions were probably inflated by deterioration in the control arm, and the F and P printed for the intrinsic-regulation interaction do not correspond to each other. A second trial had a no-training arm and did not give it the motivation instrument (Anderson et al., 2026), so nothing can be said from it.

A comparison with no exercise cannot separate the game from the exercise. In the included set, the only trial that favours the exergame arm on more than one subscale is this one. [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] That sentence was wrong: a second trial also has two subscales on which the game arm was higher (Ngo et al., 2026). What is true is narrower: this is the only included trial with more than one subscale in favour of the game arm and none against it.

3.5 Thread 2: population and health status

Rests on: six studies at tier A; one of doubtful eligibility.

Figure 5. Included studies by population group and coded direction, marked by overall risk of bias. Generated from evidence-map.csv (derived from extraction.csv and the Overall rows of rob.csv), 2026-11-28. Study IDs as in Figure 3. The dagger marks the trial kept as doubtful by the user’s decision.

Four trials are in healthy adults, and their codes are favours exergame (two), mixed (one) and none (one, the doubtful trial). The one trial in older adults (Huang et al., 2025) and the one in adolescents (Tunc et al., 2026) each have no coded direction. No population group other than healthy adults has more than one included trial, so nothing can be said about whether results differ by age or condition. No included trial recruited people with a neurological, cardiometabolic, oncological or mental-health condition; that is an absence in six open-access trials and not a statement about the field.

3.6 Thread 3: platform

Rests on: six studies at tier A; one of doubtful eligibility.

Three trials used a console or camera motion game, with codes of favours exergame (Anderson et al., 2026), mixed (Ngo et al., 2026) and none (Huang et al., 2025). One used exercise equipment with a game seen through a headset (Liu et al., 2025), one a headset game the paper does not name (Nikolova et al., 2025), and one a balance board and phone-camera games (Tunc et al., 2026). With one trial each, nothing can be said about platforms other than console or camera games, and within that group the three results differ along with their comparators, instruments and populations. The evidence does not show whether platform matters. Setting the doubtful trial aside leaves no included trial coded as a headset game.

3.7 Thread 4: follow-up and adherence

Rests on: two studies at tier A for follow-up, one of them of doubtful eligibility; one study for adherence.

Two trials measured motivation after the programme ended. One reports the same single BREQ-2 score one month later, with a between-group P read as 1.000 (Huang et al., 2025). The other reports its composite at five months, 3.92 (0.49) against 3.12 (0.43), with no between-group test at that time point (Nikolova et al., 2025). Both are totals of unstated construction, so neither supports a statement about direction at follow-up. Without the doubtful trial, one study remains and this is a single-study finding. Four trials report no follow-up.

Fewer than two trials report adherence in a way that can be compared between arms. One reports that everyone analysed in both training arms completed all 12 sessions (Anderson et al., 2026), which is the same in both arms and excludes those who dropped out. Whether adherence moves with motivation cannot be addressed from the included trials.

3.8 Thread 5: what is measured as motivation

Rests on: six studies at tier A; one of doubtful eligibility.

Three trials used a version of the BREQ (Huang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Nikolova et al., 2025), one the IMI (Anderson et al., 2026), one the Sport Motivation Scale (Ngo et al., 2026) and one the MSPPA (Tunc et al., 2026). No included trial used a need-satisfaction scale.

Three of the six report only a total or composite score (Huang et al., 2025; Nikolova et al., 2025; Tunc et al., 2026). Each of these instruments includes amotivation alongside more autonomous forms of motivation, and none of the three papers says how the total treats items that point the other way. This is the main reason the review cannot code a direction for half of its trials. The three trials that report subscales are the three with a coded direction.

Where subscales are reported, any difference between arms is on intrinsic or identified forms of motivation [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] Where subscales are reported, all three trials show a difference on an intrinsic or identified form of motivation: interest and enjoyment (Anderson et al., 2026), intrinsic motivation to know and to accomplish (Ngo et al., 2026), identified and intrinsic regulation (Liu et al., 2025). In one of the three the game arm was also higher on external regulation, which the protocol counts as unfavourable (Ngo et al., 2026); the earlier wording left that out. The IMI has no amotivation or introjected subscale. In the two trials that measured them, neither amotivation nor introjected regulation was reported as different between arms, though one prints a borderline value for amotivation in its table and describes only a main effect of time in its text (Liu et al., 2025). That is three trials, two of them rated high, using three instruments.

The trial of doubtful eligibility. Nikolova et al. (2025) is kept in the review marked doubtful, by the user’s decision at the second gate. Its paper never names the game or the headset and never says body movement is the game input; it meets I1 only under amendment A6, on the authors’ label. Both judges ruled it eligible under A6 and neither found new text either way. Two other included trials carried screening doubts that the judges cleared from the text: for Tunc et al. (2026), an appendix fetched before extraction gives the movement input and a score for each game; for Huang et al. (2025), the table gives the instrument’s means for both arms at both later time points.

3.9 Reporting biases

No registry was searched, so unpublished trials were not looked for. Three trials cite a registration (Huang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Tunc et al., 2026); the content of the registrations is not in the saved texts, so no registered outcome was compared with a reported one. One excluded trial (pm-42247423) registered motivation as an outcome and says it will be reported separately; that report was not found. The search required a motivation term in the title, abstract or index terms, which favours trials whose motivation result was worth putting in the abstract.

3.10 Certainty of evidence

Outcome Studies (randomized) Certainty (GRADE) Reasons
Motivation at end of programme, exergame against a non-exergame arm 6 trials ([computed: 257]) Very low Risk of bias: 4 of 6 high overall, none low in any domain. Inconsistency: directions differ and three cannot be coded. Indirectness: instruments, comparators and populations differ; one comparison is with no exercise. Imprecision: small trials, no pooled estimate. Publication bias suspected from the search design
Motivation at follow-up 2 trials Not rated Both report a total of unstated construction; one is of doubtful eligibility
Adherence 1 trial Not rated A single study, identical in both arms among completers

Every included study is tier A, so no rating is withheld for lack of a full text.

4. Discussion

4.1 Interpretation

The included trials do not answer the question. Two of six favour the exergame arm by their own test, both at high risk of bias, one of them against a control arm that did no exercise and one on a single subscale measured once. One is mixed. Three report a score that cannot be given a direction. No trial favours the comparator. [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] “Cannot be given a direction” must not be read as “showed nothing”: one of the three reported no difference between arms on its total (between-group P read as 0.936 at the end of the programme and 1.000 a month later) (Huang et al., 2025), and both of its judges first coded it as no between-group difference. One reported a difference in change scores and in a baseline-adjusted analysis but not in final scores, and was first coded as favouring the game arm (Tunc et al., 2026). Both codes were changed to other during appraisal under amendment A11, by agents, without an individual ruling from the user (section 2.7). As first coded the counts were three favouring, one no difference, one mixed and one uncoded. Under either coding the answer below is the same. Counting these is vote-counting over small trials and is a weak basis for any statement; the counts are given because they are all there is.

This is not evidence that exergames do not affect motivation. It is six small trials that measured motivation as one outcome among several and, in half of them, reported it in a form that cannot be interpreted. No other evidence was consulted, so the review does not place this in the context of earlier work.

Sensitivity to risk of bias. With the four trials rated high set aside, two remain: one mixed (Ngo et al., 2026) and one with no coded direction [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] whose total score showed no difference between arms and has no coded direction (Huang et al., 2025). No trial coded as favouring the exergame arm remains, under either coding. The table below gives the other conclusions without the high-risk trials.

4.2 Limitations of the evidence

  • Four of six trials are at high risk of bias, mostly from more dropout in the game arm analysed by completers.
  • Three of six report motivation only as a total and do not say how it treats items that point the other way (for one of them the score range is given and the scoring rule is not).
  • Samples are small, from 25 to 66 randomized.
  • Comparators differ in kind, and one trial compares a game with no exercise at all.
  • Four of six trials are in healthy young adults.
  • Several papers contain internal inconsistencies in the motivation results themselves: different randomized totals in abstract and text (Huang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025), sample sizes in a table that differ from the text (Anderson et al., 2026), change scores that do not follow from means (Tunc et al., 2026) and a mean above the scale maximum (Nikolova et al., 2025).
  • One included report comes from a journal not indexed in PubMed and has no DOI (Nikolova et al., 2025).

4.3 Limitations of this review

conduct-disclosure.md is the full account. The main points:

  • Machine-conducted. Screening, extraction and risk-of-bias rating were done by agents. The two screeners, and the two judges, are instances of one model and share its blind spots.
  • 21 reports were not retrieved and could not be assessed; one of them both screeners would have included on its abstract. The included set is drawn from open-access reports only.
  • Narrow by design. Only randomized trials from 2024 onward with a named multi-item instrument. The date limit, the limit of roughly 150 records at screening and backward-only citation searching were set to keep the run small; the last two were set by the operator who launched the run and accepted by the user. The review says nothing about earlier trials, non-randomized or qualitative work, single-session studies, enjoyment measured alone, or which game features motivate.
  • The search probably overstates benefit, because motivation had to be named in the title, abstract or index terms. Trials described only as “serious games” were not searched for. Two sources were searched; six named databases, registries and grey literature were not.
  • The protocol changed thirteen times after approval, each change dated and approved by the user, one of them (A1) only after the fact. Four were made after appraisal had begun, and they changed one overall rating and three direction codes.
  • Five excluded reports were read as preprints (oa-W4413422558, pm-42261097, oa-W4395005416, oa-W7164739728, s1-oa-W4411350775) and one as an accepted manuscript (pm-38801680); a published version could differ.
  • Three included trials cite a registration and none was read. No registry was consulted, so no registered outcome was compared with a reported one. This is a gap in the review, not in the trials. [Moved here from section 4.4 after audit.]
  • An appendix was fetched for one included report after screening; the screeners did not see it.
  • The retrieval route added by A2 came with a plugin update made between the second gate being written and answered.
  • Not registered. No protocol was registered before the review began.

4.4 Implications

For practice: the included trials give no basis for expecting an exergame programme to raise, or to lower, exercise motivation compared with conventional exercise.

For research, three two absences in the included set, each bounded by this search [Corrected after audit, 2026-11-28] (a third item, about registrations, described a gap in this review and has moved to section 4.3): half report a total score without saying how it was formed; none reports motivation and comparable adherence in both arms. These are statements about six trials, not about the field.
